claim: Cisplatin is a highly effective anticancer agent that primarily functions through covalent-binding to purine bases, resulting in DNA crosslinks, activation of repair pathways, formation of double stranded breaks (DSBs), increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and apoptosis.
source: Cisplatin is a highly effective anticancer agent that primarily functions through covalent-binding to purine bases, resulting in DNA crosslinks, activation of repair pathways, formation of double stranded breaks (DSBs), increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and apoptosis (Dasari and Tchounwou, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dasari and Tchounwou, 2014

claim: Cisplatin treatment is associated with dose-limiting toxicities such as oto- and nephrotoxicity.
source: However, cisplatin treatment is associated with a variety of side effects, including dose-limiting toxicities such as oto- and nephrotoxicity (Brock et al., 2012; Pabla and Dong, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brock et al., 2012 and Pabla and Dong, 2008

claim: Ototoxicity is permanent in humans.
source: While ototoxicity is permanent in humans, nephrotoxicity can be acute or chronic in nature, and can sometimes demonstrate partial recovery (Brock et al., 2012; Brock et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brock et al., 2012 and Brock et al., 1991

claim: Nephrotoxicity can be acute or chronic in nature, and can sometimes demonstrate partial recovery.
source: While ototoxicity is permanent in humans, nephrotoxicity can be acute or chronic in nature, and can sometimes demonstrate partial recovery (Brock et al., 2012; Brock et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brock et al., 2012 and Brock et al., 1991

claim: Approximately 61% of pediatric patients treated with cisplatin will experience hearing loss according to the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) criteria.
source: Approximately 61% of pediatric patients treated with cisplatin will experience hearing loss according to the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) criteria (Knight et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knight et al., 2005

claim: Cisplatin treatment is correlated with changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in approximately 20–30% of patients.
source: While estimates vary greatly, cisplatin treatment is similarly correlated with changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in approximately 20–30% of patients (Hartmann et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hartmann et al., 1999

claim: Hypomagnesemia is a common and persistent side-effect of cisplatin treatment.
source: Hypomagnesemia, or low serum magnesium levels, is a common and persistent side-effect of cisplatin treatment (Stöhr et al., 2007), which can lead to seizures, mood changes, tremors, and myocardial infarction (Lajer and Daugaard, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stöhr et al., 2007 and Lajer and Daugaard, 1999

claim: Nephrotoxicity occurs in approximately one third of patients, detectable approximately 10 days after cisplatin therapy.
source: Nephrotoxicity was observed in some of the first human trials using cisplatin (Higby et al., 1974), and occurs in approximately one third of patients, detectable approximately 10 days after cisplatin therapy (Crona et al., 2017; Gonzales-Vitale et al., 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Higby et al., 1974, Crona et al., 2017, and Gonzales-Vitale et al., 1977

claim: Renal damage appears to be at least partially reversible for some patients, usually in those that received low cumulative doses, or were young at the time of treatment.
source: Unlike ototoxicity, renal damage appears to be at least partially reversible for some patients, usually in those that received low cumulative doses, or were young at the time of treatment (Brock et al., 1991; Latcha et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brock et al., 1991 and Latcha et al., 2016

claim: There are no FDA-approved drugs to protect against cisplatin ototoxicity.
source: Currently, there are no FDA-approved drugs to protect against cisplatin ototoxicity.
evidence: Statement of current clinical status

claim: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) has shown promise as an oto- and nephroprotective agent in multiple preclinical models.
source: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is an antioxidant that has shown promise as an oto- and nephroprotective agent in multiple preclinical models (Dickey et al., 2005; Luo et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dickey et al., 2005, Luo et al., 2008, and Wu et al., 2006

claim: NAC acts primarily by reducing the elevated levels of ROS that may induce cellular damage, as well as by direct inactivation by complexing with cisplatin in the cell.
source: In the context of cisplatin exposure, studies suggest that NAC acts primarily by reducing the elevated levels of ROS that may induce cellular damage, as well as by direct inactivation by complexing with cisplatin in the cell (Dickey et al., 2005; Norman et al., 1992; Rushworth and Megson, 2014; Sooriyaarachchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dickey et al., 2005, Norman et al., 1992, Rushworth and Megson, 2014, and Sooriyaarachchi et al., 2016

claim: Sodium thiosulfate (STS) has demonstrated otoprotective capacity preclinically, and in several pediatric Phase III clinical trials.
source: Sodium thiosulfate (STS) has also demonstrated otoprotective capacity preclinically, and in several pediatric Phase III clinical trials (ex. NCT00716976, NCT00652132) (Brock et al., 2018; Dickey et al., 2005; Doolittle et al., 2001; Freyer et al., 2017; Muldoon et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brock et al., 2018, Dickey et al., 2005, Doolittle et al., 2001, Freyer et al., 2017, and Muldoon et al., 2000

claim: STS is not typically used clinically because of its detrimental impact on overall survival in a subset of patients.
source: However, STS is not typically used clinically because of its detrimental impact on overall survival in a subset of patients (Freyer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Freyer et al., 2017

claim: The zebrafish larva is uniquely suited to identifying novel protective compounds through drug screening, combining the advantages of cell lines and vertebrate models.
source: The zebrafish larva is uniquely suited to identifying novel protective compounds through drug screening, combining the advantages of cell lines (extremely small size suitable for multi-well plates, ease of chemical exposure) and vertebrate models (functional organ systems, genetic conservation) (MacRae and Peterson, 2015; Zon and Peterson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to MacRae and Peterson, 2015 and Zon and Peterson, 2005

claim: A zebrafish larval drug screen identified the natural product, visnagin, as a cardioprotectant against short-term anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicty.
source: Indeed, a zebrafish larval drug screen identified the natural product, visnagin, as a cardioprotectant against short-term anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicty (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014

claim: Zebrafish larvae as young as four days post-fertilization (dpf) possess a functional pronephros structure and a sophisticated oto-vestibulary system including an inner ear structure with multiple sensory placodes.
source: Zebrafish larvae as young as four days post-fertilization (dpf) possess a functional pronephros structure (a primitive kidney that resembles the two nephrons, running along the length of the larva) and a sophisticated oto-vestibulary system including an inner ear structure with multiple sensory placodes (Baxendale and Whitfield, 2016; Drummond and Davidson, 2010; Hentschel et al., 2005; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baxendale and Whitfield, 2016, Drummond and Davidson, 2010, Hentschel et al., 2005, and Whitfield et al., 2002

claim: The zebrafish possesses a lateral line consisting of clusters of hair cells (called neuromasts) for sensing water movement, which are analogous to the hair cells found in mammalian cochlea.
source: Equally important for in vivo drug screening, like many teleosts, the zebrafish possesses a lateral line consisting of clusters of hair cells (called neuromasts) for sensing water movement, which are analogous to the hair cells found in mammalian cochlea (Raible and Kruse, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raible and Kruse, 2000

claim: Neuromast hair cells are susceptible to ototoxins like cisplatin.
source: Neuromast hair cells are susceptible to ototoxins like cisplatin (Ou et al., 2007) and the lateral line is superficial and accessible, making zebrafish an excellent in vivo ototoxicity screening system.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ou et al., 2007

claim: Cisplatin treatment results in a dose-dependent decrease in neuromast health in zebrafish larvae.
source: A dose-dependent relationship between cisplatin dose and peak height (PH) green fluorescence was observed, which correlated to YO-PRO-1 neuromast staining.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: The EC50 for cisplatin-induced neuromast toxicity was calculated to be 0.027 mM.
source: The EC50, or effective concentration at which half of the maximal neuromast PH fluorescence was calculated to be 0.027 mM, according to a four-parameter log-logistic model (see Materials and methods for supporting information).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data using statistical modeling

claim: Cisplatin treatment results in a dose-dependent decrease in HK-2 cell viability.
source: Results displayed a dose-dependent decrease in HK-2 cell viability with increasing cisplatin dose.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: The Sigma LOPAC1280 library was screened for potential protective agents using a parallel two-pronged approach in zebrafish neuromasts and HK-2 human proximal tubule cells.
source: Following the establishment of predictable dose–response curves for cisplatin-induced oto- and nephrotoxicity, the Sigma LOPAC1280 library was screened for potential protective agents. This was accomplished with a parallel two-pronged approach using our assays described above in zebrafish neuromasts and HK-2 human proximal tubule cells.
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: 22 compounds were identified that were protective against cisplatin nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
source: Following completion of both screens, we identified 22 'hits': compounds that were protective against cisplatin nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (resulting in viability values corresponding to 0.9–1.1X of the no drug control value).
evidence: Results from the drug screen described in the manuscript

claim: Dopamine and L-mimosine were revealed to be two of the most protective compounds based on the results from the in vitro and in vivo drug screen.
source: Dopamine and L-mimosine were revealed to be two of the most protective compounds, based on the results from the in vitro and in vivo drug screen.
evidence: Results from the drug screen

claim: Treatment with dopamine at 0.03 mM resulted in significant neuromast protection compared to larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
source: Based on these preliminary results, we determined that a 12 hr pretreatment with the protective agent prior to cisplatin treatment was ideal, so all subsequent experiments used this time course. Following this schedule, we observed significant neuromast protection with dopamine at 0.03 mM, L-mimosine at both 0.03 and 0.04 mM, and with the combination of dopamine and L-mimosine at 0.02 mM each (Figure 3a), when compared to larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Treatment with L-mimosine at both 0.03 and 0.04 mM resulted in significant neuromast protection compared to larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
source: Based on these preliminary results, we determined that a 12 hr pretreatment with the protective agent prior to cisplatin treatment was ideal, so all subsequent experiments used this time course. Following this schedule, we observed significant neuromast protection with dopamine at 0.03 mM, L-mimosine at both 0.03 and 0.04 mM, and with the combination of dopamine and L-mimosine at 0.02 mM each (Figure 3a), when compared to larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Treatment with the combination of dopamine and L-mimosine at 0.02 mM each resulted in significant neuromast protection compared to larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
source: Based on these preliminary results, we determined that a 12 hr pretreatment with the protective agent prior to cisplatin treatment was ideal, so all subsequent experiments used this time course. Following this schedule, we observed significant neuromast protection with dopamine at 0.03 mM, L-mimosine at both 0.03 and 0.04 mM, and with the combination of dopamine and L-mimosine at 0.02 mM each (Figure 3a), when compared to larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Treatment with the full dose of cisplatin (0.02 mM) and either L-mimosine at 0.04 mM or the combination of dopamine and L-mimosine at 0.02 mM each resulted in neuromast fluorescence that was not significantly different from the larvae treated with 0.01 mM cisplatin alone.
source: Treatment with the full dose of cisplatin (100%, or 0.02 mM) and either L-mimosine at 0.04 mM or the combination of dopamine and L-mimosine at 0.02 mM each resulted in neuromast fluorescence that was not significantly different from the larvae treated with 0.01 mM cisplatin alone (the 50% dose).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Use of these protective agents could allow for larger doses of cisplatin to be given without further damage to the hair cells.
source: These data suggest that use of these protective agents could allow for larger doses of cisplatin to be given without further damage to the hair cells, which could have potential therapeutic benefit.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing protection at higher cisplatin doses

claim: Pretreatment with dopamine or L-mimosine protects inner ear hair cells from cisplatin-induced damage.
source: Qualitatively, the hair cells appear more plentiful and more structurally intact in the groups that were pretreated with dopamine and L-mimosine in comparison to the cisplatin alone group.
evidence: Qualitative observation from confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 4a-d

claim: Cisplatin alone decreases the prolate ellipticity of inner ear hair cells in comparison with control hair cells.
source: Results demonstrate that cisplatin alone decreases the prolate ellipticity in comparison with control hair cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4e

claim: Pretreatment with either dopamine or L-mimosine significantly increased the prolate ellipticity of inner ear hair cells, in comparison with cisplatin treatment alone.
source: Pretreatment with either dopamine or L-mimosine significantly increased the prolate ellipticity, in comparison with cisplatin treatment alone.
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantitative data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Hair cells from larvae that were pretreated with dopamine or L-mimosine had prolate ellipticity that was not significantly different from hair cells of control larvae.
source: Importantly, hair cells from larvae that were pretreated with dopamine or L-mimosine had prolate ellipticity that was not significantly different from hair cells of control larvae (Figure 4e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantitative data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Dopamine and L-mimosine pretreatments resulted in hair cell numbers that were higher than those observed in larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
source: It should be noted that the same trend was observed, where dopamine and L-mimosine pretreatments resulted in hair cell numbers that were higher than those observed in larvae treated with cisplatin alone.
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4f

claim: Cisplatin treatment resulted in a decreased change in fluorescence over time, indicative of decreased GFR.
source: Cisplatin treatment resulted in a decreased change in fluorescence over time, indicative of decreased GFR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a

claim: There was a significant decrease in fluorescence in the control group over 2 hr demonstrating normal excretion, but not in the group that was treated for 24 hr with 0.125 mM cisplatin.
source: Following inulin injection, there was a significant decrease in fluorescence in the control group over 2 hr demonstrating normal excretion, but not in the group that was treated for 24 hr with 0.125 mM cisplatin (Figure 5a).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5a

claim: When larvae were pretreated with either dopamine or L-mimosine prior to cisplatin treatment, there was a detectable decrease in fluorescence over 2 hr, demonstrating enhanced GFR.
source: However, when the larvae were pretreated with either dopamine or L-mimosine prior to cisplatin treatment, there was a detectable decrease in fluorescence over 2 hr, demonstrating enhanced GFR (Figure 5, representative images of inulin-injected larvae can be found in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.)
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1d

claim: Both 24 and 72 hr treatment with 0.125 mM cisplatin did not cause any distinct visible changes to the pronephros histology.
source: Results suggested that both 24 and 72 hr treatment with 0.125 mM cisplatin did not cause any distinct visible changes to the pronephros histology (24 hpt data: Figures 5b–e, 72 hpt data: Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figures 5b-e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-d

claim: In all treatment groups, and at both 24 and 48 hpt, dopamine and L-mimosine either had no effect on cancer cell viability, or significantly increased the cytotoxic effects of cisplatin.
source: In all treatment groups, and at both 24 and 48 hpt, dopamine and L-mimosine either had no effect on cancer cell viability, or significantly increased the cytotoxic effects of cisplatin (48 hpt data: Figures 6a–f, 24 hpt data: Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–f).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figures 6a-f and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-f

claim: Cisplatin treatment increased levels of apoptosis in NBL cells.
source: We found increased levels of apoptosis in NBL cells treated with cisplatin alone (Figure 6g), and pretreatment with either 0.03 mM dopamine or L-mimosine did not reduce the levels of apoptosis.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6g

claim: Pretreatment with either 0.03 mM dopamine or L-mimosine did not reduce the levels of apoptosis induced by cisplatin in NBL cells.
source: We found increased levels of apoptosis in NBL cells treated with cisplatin alone (Figure 6g), and pretreatment with either 0.03 mM dopamine or L-mimosine did not reduce the levels of apoptosis.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6g

claim: Cisplatin treatment increased DSB formation in both SK-N-AS and LAN5 NBL cell lines.
source: Results in both SK-N-AS and LAN5 NBL cell lines demonstrate that cisplatin treatment increased DSB formation, and pretreatment with either dopamine or L-mimosine did not reduce these levels (Quantification of DSBs: Figure 6h,i, Representative images of SK-N-AS cells: Figure 6j).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 6h-j

claim: Pretreatment with either dopamine or L-mimosine did not reduce DSB formation induced by cisplatin in NBL cell lines.
source: Results in both SK-N-AS and LAN5 NBL cell lines demonstrate that cisplatin treatment increased DSB formation, and pretreatment with either dopamine or L-mimosine did not reduce these levels (Quantification of DSBs: Figure 6h,i, Representative images of SK-N-AS cells: Figure 6j).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 6h-j

claim: In SK-N-AS cells, L-mimosine pretreatment increased DSB formation over cisplatin treatment alone.
source: However, there were differences between the cell lines based on their response to L-mimosine pretreatment: in SK-N-AS cells, L-mimosine pretreatment increased DSB formation over cisplatin treatment alone, while in LAN5 cells, the same treatment resulted in a slight, but significant decrease in DSB formation compared with cisplatin alone.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data

claim: In LAN5 cells, L-mimosine pretreatment resulted in a slight, but significant decrease in DSB formation compared with cisplatin alone.
source: However, there were differences between the cell lines based on their response to L-mimosine pretreatment: in SK-N-AS cells, L-mimosine pretreatment increased DSB formation over cisplatin treatment alone, while in LAN5 cells, the same treatment resulted in a slight, but significant decrease in DSB formation compared with cisplatin alone.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data

claim: Individuals that received STS had significantly less hearing loss (45 vs. 84%, p=0.00022).
source: While the individuals that received STS had significantly less hearing loss (45 vs. 84%, p=0.00022), the individuals with disseminated disease at the time of diagnosis had worse overall survival when treated with STS (45% vs. 84%, respectively, p=0.009).
evidence: Clinical trial data cited from Freyer et al., 2017

claim: Individuals with disseminated disease at the time of diagnosis had worse overall survival when treated with STS (45% vs. 84%, respectively, p=0.009).
source: While the individuals that received STS had significantly less hearing loss (45 vs. 84%, p=0.00022), the individuals with disseminated disease at the time of diagnosis had worse overall survival when treated with STS (45% vs. 84%, respectively, p=0.009).
evidence: Clinical trial data cited from Freyer et al., 2017

claim: STS functions as a protective agent by both scavenging ROS and forming a direct complex with cisplatin, inactivating the drug.
source: It is not currently known why this difference in overall survival with STS treatment occurred, but it is worth noting that STS is known to function as a protective agent in several ways, both scavenging ROS and forming a direct complex with cisplatin, inactivating the drug (Bijarnia et al., 2015; Sooriyaarachchi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bijarnia et al., 2015 and Sooriyaarachchi et al., 2012

claim: There were seven compounds in the Sigma LOPAC1280 library that were hits in the in vitro nephrotoxicity assay that were toxic at the same dose to the zebrafish larvae.
source: For example, there were seven compounds in the Sigma LOPAC1280 library that were hits in the in vitro nephrotoxicity assay that were toxic at the same dose to the zebrafish larvae (listed in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Results from the drug screen

claim: NAC was a hit in the ototoxicity screen, but not the nephrotoxicity screen.
source: For example, NAC was a hit in the ototoxicity screen, but not the nephrotoxicity screen.
evidence: Results from the drug screen

claim: A study of both aminoglycoside- and cisplatin-induced zebrafish lateral line toxicity identified paroxetine and fluspirilene among the 10 hits emphasized.
source: The multiple appearances of dopaminergic and serotonergic pathway modulators in this study (Table 1) is supported by similar findings in a study of both aminoglycoside- and cisplatin-induced zebrafish lateral line toxicity (Vlasits et al., 2012). Among the 10 hits emphasized in the Vlasits et al., study were paroxetine, a selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and fluspirilene, an antipsychotic compound that acts as an antagonist at the D2 dopamine receptor (Vlasits et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vlasits et al., 2012

claim: Trifluoperazine dihydrochloride, a D2-receptor antagonist was a hit in both assays in this study.
source: For example, trifluoperazine dihydrochloride, a D2-receptor antagonist was a hit in both assays in this study.
evidence: Results from the drug screen

claim: 15% of the Sigma LOPAC1280 library consists of compounds that would interact with either the dopaminergic or serotonergic pathway (9% and 6%, respectively).
source: Of note, 15% of the Sigma LOPAC1280 library consists of compounds that would interact with either the dopaminergic or serotonergic pathway (9% and 6%, respectively).
evidence: Analysis of the drug library composition

claim: D1 and D2-like receptors are both present in the mammalian inner ear.
source: D1 and D2-like receptors are both present in the mammalian inner ear (Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011) and kidney (Harris and Zhang, 2012; Jose et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011, Harris and Zhang, 2012, and Jose et al., 1992

claim: D1 and D2-like receptors are both present in the mammalian kidney.
source: D1 and D2-like receptors are both present in the mammalian inner ear (Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011) and kidney (Harris and Zhang, 2012; Jose et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris and Zhang, 2012 and Jose et al., 1992

claim: Organic anion transporter 2 (OCT2), the transporter that seems to play a role in cisplatin uptake into both renal tubule and cochlear cells, is also capable of transporting dopamine.
source: Another point of interest is that organic anion transporter 2 (OCT2), the transporter that seems to play a role in cisplatin uptake into both renal tubule and cochlear cells, is also capable of transporting dopamine (Ciarimboli et al., 2010; Filipski et al., 2008; Filipski et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ciarimboli et al., 2010, Filipski et al., 2008, and Filipski et al., 2009

claim: There is strong evidence that dopamine protects auditory nerves from glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity.
source: Interestingly, there is also strong evidence that dopamine protects auditory nerves from glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity (Lendvai et al., 2011; Ruel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lendvai et al., 2011 and Ruel et al., 2001

claim: Increases in intracellular cAMP seem to provide nephroprotection in some studies.
source: Although the hypothesis that oto- and nephroprotection may be mediated by increased dopamine signaling still needs to be confirmed, it is possible that dopamine could bind to the D1 or D5 receptors present in the inner ear and/or pronephros structure, causing increases in intracellular cAMP, which seems to provide nephroprotection in some studies (Gillies et al., 2015; Hans et al., 1990; Palmieri et al., 1993) and cochlear nerve protection from noise-induced hearing damage (Darrow et al., 2007; Lendvai et al., 2011; Ruel et al., 2001; Oestreicher et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gillies et al., 2015, Hans et al., 1990, and Palmieri et al., 1993

claim: Increases in intracellular cAMP provide cochlear nerve protection from noise-induced hearing damage.
source: Although the hypothesis that oto- and nephroprotection may be mediated by increased dopamine signaling still needs to be confirmed, it is possible that dopamine could bind to the D1 or D5 receptors present in the inner ear and/or pronephros structure, causing increases in intracellular cAMP, which seems to provide nephroprotection in some studies (Gillies et al., 2015; Hans et al., 1990; Palmieri et al., 1993) and cochlear nerve protection from noise-induced hearing damage (Darrow et al., 2007; Lendvai et al., 2011; Ruel et al., 2001; Oestreicher et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Darrow et al., 2007, Lendvai et al., 2011, Ruel et al., 2001, and Oestreicher et al., 1997

claim: L-DOPA (levodopa) is currently used to treat Parkinson's disease.
source: L-DOPA (levodopa), the biosynthetic precursor to dopamine, is currently used to treat Parkinson's disease, which is mostly caused by the pathological loss of dopaminergic neurons in regions of the brain (Salat and Tolosa, 2013; Sethi, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Salat and Tolosa, 2013 and Sethi, 2010

claim: Individuals with Parkinson's disease have significantly worse hearing in comparison with age-matched controls.
source: Individuals with Parkinson's disease have significantly worse hearing in comparison with age-matched controls (Vitale et al., 2012), a symptom of this neurodegenerative disorder that is partially improved by dopaminergic treatment (Pisani et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vitale et al., 2012 and Pisani et al., 2015

claim: Hearing loss in Parkinson's disease is partially improved by dopaminergic treatment.
source: Individuals with Parkinson's disease have significantly worse hearing in comparison with age-matched controls (Vitale et al., 2012), a symptom of this neurodegenerative disorder that is partially improved by dopaminergic treatment (Pisani et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pisani et al., 2015

claim: L-DOPA was a hit in the otoprotection assay, but not the nephroprotection assay.
source: In the present study, L-DOPA was a hit in the otoprotection assay, but not the nephroprotection assay, which may have been a result of only testing one dose at one time point in the initial screen; however, the potential utility of this clinically utilized compound should be the topic for further investigation.
evidence: Results from the drug screen

claim: Researchers have previously attempted to use low dose dopamine (0.5–3 µg/kg/min) to increase renal blood flow and potentially protect the kidneys from cisplatin.
source: In terms of potential nephroprotective effects, researchers have previously attempted to use low dose dopamine (0.5–3 µg/kg/min) to increase renal blood flow and potentially protect the kidneys from cisplatin (Kellum, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kellum, 1997

claim: The results of multiple studies do not currently support the use of dopamine as a nephroprotectant.
source: The results of multiple studies were conflicting, and do not currently support the use of dopamine as a nephroprotectant (Crona et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crona et al., 2017

claim: Fenoldopam, a selective D1 receptor agonist reduced post-operative acute kidney injury.
source: One study found that fenoldopam, a selective D1 receptor agonist reduced post-operative acute kidney injury (Gillies et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gillies et al., 2015

claim: Teleost hair cells (both lateral line and inner ear) regenerate, while mammalian hair cells do not.
source: Another important difference between human inner ear hair cells and zebrafish hair cells is that teleost hair cells (both lateral line and inner ear) regenerate, while mammalian hair cells do not (Monroe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Monroe et al., 2015

claim: The study screened 1280 compounds and identified 22 that were both oto- and nephroprotective.
source: Using a two-pronged drug screen employing the zebrafish lateral line as an in vivo readout for ototoxicity and kidney cell-based nephrotoxicity assay, we screened 1280 compounds and identified 22 that were both oto- and nephroprotective.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from the drug screen

claim: Dopamine and L-mimosine protected the hair cells in the zebrafish otic vesicle from cisplatin-induced damage.
source: Dopamine and L-mimosine protected the hair cells in the zebrafish otic vesicle from cisplatin-induced damage and preserved zebrafish larval glomerular filtration.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Dopamine and L-mimosine preserved zebrafish larval glomerular filtration.
source: Dopamine and L-mimosine protected the hair cells in the zebrafish otic vesicle from cisplatin-induced damage and preserved zebrafish larval glomerular filtration.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Dopamine and L-mimosine did not abrogate the cytotoxic effects of cisplatin on human cancer cells.
source: Importantly, these compounds did not abrogate the cytotoxic effects of cisplatin on human cancer cells.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Plasma cisplatin levels range from approximately 1–10 µg/mL over the initial 24 hr period following administration, which translates to 0.0033 mM-0.033 mM.
source: Human studies suggest that over the initial 24 hr period following administration, plasma cisplatin levels range from approximately 1–10 µg/mL, which translates to 0.0033 mM-0.033 mM (Lanvers-Kaminsky et al., 2006; Rajkumar et al., 2016), well within the range of what we used experimentally.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lanvers-Kaminsky et al., 2006 and Rajkumar et al., 2016

claim: Casper zebrafish were used throughout the study due to enhanced optical clarity and utility in fluorescence-based experimentation, without the need for phenylthiourea (PTU) treatment.
source: Casper zebrafish were used throughout the study due to enhanced optical clarity and utility in fluorescence-based experimentation, without the need for phenylthiourea (PTU) treatment, which has been shown to influence both behavior and neural crest development (Bohnsack et al., 2011; Parker et al., 2013).
evidence: Methodological justification with citations to Bohnsack et al., 2011 and Parker et al., 2013

claim: Other groups have used the casper mutant larvae to observe the zebrafish auditory system and demonstrate similar ototoxicity responses in both casper mutants and wild-type larvae.
source: Other groups have also used the casper mutant larvae to observe the zebrafish auditory system (Wisniowiecki et al., 2016) and demonstrate similar ototoxicity responses in both casper mutants and wild-type larvae (d'd'Alençon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wisniowiecki et al., 2016 and d'd'Alençon et al., 2010

claim: YO-PRO-1 is a carbocyanine nucleic acid stain that labels the nuclei of viable hair cells.
source: YO-PRO-1 is a carbocyanine nucleic acid stain that labels the nuclei of viable hair cells (Baxendale and Whitfield, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baxendale and Whitfield, 2016

claim: Inulin is a polysaccharide that is excreted exclusively through the nephron.
source: Inulin is a polysaccharide that is excreted exclusively through the nephron, so when this compound is injected into the circulation, decreases in vascular fluorescence over time correspond with GFR (Hentschel et al., 2005; Rider et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hentschel et al., 2005 and Rider et al., 2012

claim: Levels of γH2AX antibody staining 24 hr following cisplatin exposure has been reported to correlate with the long-term viability of the cells following treatment.
source: Levels of γH2AX antibody staining 24 hr following cisplatin exposure has been reported to correlate with the long-term viability of the cells following treatment (Olive and Banáth, 2009).
